speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRAIRIE PROVINCES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF ACTION TO CONTINUE SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding the north prairie regional air route.
The air transport board has made an extensive review of western regional air services. The board's report makes it clear that certain regional routes, including the present north prairie route, cannot operate on a self sustaining basis. The report also indicates that the volume of traffic from point to point is extremely uneven and that some points are not, in fact, making enough use of the air service to justify continuation; while at other points, although volume of use is not enough to cover losses on operation, nevertheless it is sufficient to indicate public need for and reliance upon the air service.
In the case of the north prairie route, the board reports that there is a continuing need for and community of interest in regard to air service between Regina, Saskatoon and Prince Albert, and that this segment of the route should be kept in existence. It also reported that the western segment of the route from Prince Albert onward to Edmonton is not carrying enough traffic to justify continuation and recommends the discontinuation of this segment of the route.
The present carrier, Pacific Western Airlines, has been asked whether it would be prepared to carry on the service Regina-Saskatoon-Prince Albert without subsidy but has replied in the negative. In the circumstances the matter has also been
discussed with the management of Trans-Canada Air Lines, which has indicated that it believes the Regina-Saskatoon-Prince Albert route could be integrated with its western services probably on a daily round trip basis, with very little adjustment on its part. T.C.A. management having expressed its ability and willingness, arrangements are being made for the granting of a licence for this route to T.C.A. The exact date for the grant of the licence and the plans of T.C.A. for operation have not yet been made final.
As far as can be seen at present, T.C.A. plans to operate this route with its own equipment and personnel. However, there may be a delay of a few weeks before this can take place; and in view of the desirability of maintaining continuity of service, the management of T.C.A. is presently engaged in discussions with Pacific Western to ensure that the latter is in a position to maintain service on the Regina-Saskatoon-Prince Albert route until T.C.A. is in a position to take over the licence and to operate itself. I have been assured by the management of T.C.A. that there will be no hiatus in the service.
I wish to pay tribute to the co-operative interest shown by T.C.A. in dealing with this problem, and the recognition of the requirements of public service which they have shown in their readiness to maintain this important route.
There remains the question of the south prairie route which was also dealt with in the air transport board report. I will shortly make a separate further statement on this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PRAIRIE PROVINCES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF ACTION TO CONTINUE SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will, of course, be interested in the statement the minister has just made because there has been some uncertainty in connection with this matter for some time. I would have hoped, and I am sure the house would have hoped as well, that the minister would take this opportunity to make a statement on the national air policy as well as the transcontinental air policy of the government.
The minister will remember that some time ago there was a question raised in connection with that matter by one of his own officers, and while I do not want to go into

Air Transport
it I just mention it in passing because I think many of us here would welcome a statement from the minister on these services. However, the minister has made a statement having to do with this particular prairie route arising out of studies made by the air transport board, and again I think the house would have welcomed a statement of policy in connection with regional air services. This has not been the case, but the government through the minister has made a statement concerning this particular service.
I suggest to the minister with respect that this decision, far from moving toward a national air policy, is again dealing with the matter by piecemeal surgery, as it were. Here is a company, and X speak now, of course, of Pacific Western Airlines, that has played an important part in the prairie economy, and the question that comes to mind is this. Why should we terminate a subsidy to a private concern which in five years has sustained almost $1 million in operating losses to prove the route, and instead hide the loss under the wing of public investment? T.C.A., of course, is going to take over this service, but from the evidence we received in another place this morning it is quite clear that there is going to be an operating loss for T.C.A. in this particular field. It seems to me it would have been much better to allow the regional carrier to carry on under the present circumstances in the hope that with increasing business it might have been possible in time to strengthen its financial position.
I think the minister should give an undertaking to the house that T.C.A., in taking over this service into Prince Albert, is not going to increase the cost to the taxpayer; because I have some recollection of what transpired in similar circumstances on a previous occasion. The minister will remember that when his predecessor in office, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, decontrolled certain air services because he then said that it was in the general interest of Canada, the financial position of the regional air carriers was made far worse than it had been. I am afraid that the situation here is going to be one which will hurt the regional air carriers, whereas in accordance with the Wheatcroft report the intention then, according to the expert of the government, was that these regional carriers would serve as feeders to assist the main line carriers.
I hope it will be possible for the minister to give consideration to the comments I have made.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I enter the debate on this question of interim supply purely for the purpose of making an appeal to the government with regard to the carrying on of the business of the house. Yesterday the Prime Minister sought to place upon the opposition groups the responsibility for whether or not this is a productive session, and he made statements at that time which it seems to me are astounding comments coming from him or from any other prime minister.
One of his first comments concerned the sitting hours of this house. It seems to me a strange thing that any person with the long years of experience the Prime Minister has had should leave the impression with the general public that members of parliament who are engaged in their parliamentary duties are so engaged for something less than 30 hours a week. As a matter of fact the hours which this house sits are comparable with the hours which all other legislative groups sit, both in this country and in other countries. Hon. members know, although unfortunately the public does not always know, that the hours of sitting in the house are only part of a member's duties. Hon. members also have to spend time in their offices answering mail, carrying on research, visiting various departments, taking up the problems of their constituents and attending the meetings of the committees of this house.
I	think the impression which was left yesterday that members are on a sort of holiday here was a very unfortunate impression to be left by the Prime Minister. As a matter of fact, many members of this house spend
II	or 12 hours a day in this building, and the problem we face is not going to be solved simply by extending the hours of sitting.
The Prime Minister also mentioned yesterday the matter of long question periods. I was rather intrigued with his comment about the old days when he and I sat in the house as private members, and when there were only two or three questions. If my recollection serves me aright, the Prime Minister himself never asked less than two or three questions on orders of the day, and I will say that he was very good at it.
The Prime Minister said yesterday that a whole host of questions are asked but that not one in a carload would embarrass the government. I did not know that was the

purpose of asking questions. That may have been the purpose of the Prime Minister in asking questions when he was in opposition, but I would point out that if the question period has grown, and it has, it is largely because members have not been able to get the opportunity to raise many pressing problems which are confronting their constituents, problems which they could raise with the minister concerned if we got on to the estimates. For instance, the Prime Minister said yesterday that we have spent two days on the agriculture estimates. The first day consisted of an hour and a quarter from 3.45 p.m. until 5 p.m. The second day consisted of from 11.45 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 2.30 p.m. to 5 p.m. This totals something in the neighbourhood of five hours spent on agriculture estimates, and that is the only department whose estimates have been considered and on which hon. members could ask questions. There are a host of problems, and hon. members may wait weeks or months before certain departments will come up.
Questions have been asked, too, because there are a great many important issues before the country on which there has been no opportunity for members to ascertain the government's policy, and about which the people of Canada want to know what the government intends to do; and the members of this house have the right to know this, as has the public.
I hope the impression does not go throughout the country, as a result of the Prime Minister's statement, that nothing is being done in this house. He spoke of their having 29 pieces of legislation ready. As a matter of fact I think some 43 pieces of legislation have either been passed or are somewhere in the process of being dealt with by this house. When the Prime Minister talked yesterday about a limited number of days being available for government business, my mind went back to the days when the House of Commons used to take six weeks and more on the speech from the throne and three or four weeks on the budget. The fact that the time has been limited now to ten days on the speech from the throne and nine days on the budget certainly gives a great deal more opportunity for business to be carried on.
I wish to say this, Mr. Chairman, and I am here making a plea to the government. If the business of the house is not progressing as quickly as it ought to progress, the government itself must accept the major part of the responsibility. I rose simply for the purpose of making a suggestion and it is this. A great many problems which are of concern to the members ought to be referred to committees of this house. The committee on estimates
Interim Supply
could deal with some of the departments. There is no reason why 264 or 265 members should be tied up here on some department which has interest to only a certain group of members-let us say the fisheries estimates or estimates that apply to a limited number- when by sending these estimates to a committee where the members vitally concerned could question the minister and get the answers they desire, parliament could be saved a great deal of time.
In our opinion the drug act, for instance, could have gone and should still go to a committee of the house. It would have saved a great deal of time in the house if that act had gone to a committee and it would still save a great deal of time if that act went there, where the members who are concerned about this problem could discuss it with the minister, his officials and, if necessary, the representatives of the pharmaceutical houses.

The committee at that time could have called before it the chairman of each of these two bodies and any other persons they had in mind. It could have looked into this matter. If the government and the minister concerned tell us that they have no jurisdiction, then certainly parliament has some responsibility. A committee of parliament could have looked into this matter and could have tried to resolve it. Instead of that procedure, members have been frustrated in trying to deal with a problem which to them is important, as to many of us this looks like an undermining and a weakening of the role which the publicly owned and publicly sponsored broadcasting organization is supposed to play in this country.

thing and another minister indicates it might be something different. I have a matter which I have been wishing to raise for a long time. I am not going to raise it now, though I would be perfectly within my rights in doing so. Nevertheless, I am saying to the government that unless there is some opportunity to discuss it, I shall have to take the first opportunity which presents itself, even though it means holding up interim supply at some later date.
I am referring now to the abandonment of branch lines which is taking place at such a rapid rate on the prairies. The report of the royal commission on transportation, for instance, said there are 4,300 miles of light density lines in Canada, the greater part of which is in the western area. The vice president of the C.P.R. when appearing before the royal commission stated that in the prairies there are about 2,500 miles of branch lines that will of necessity be candidates for abandonment. This is a real cause for concern. If it were only a projected abandonment the situation would not be so bad. However, at the moment in the province of Saskatchewan alone there are six lines the abandonment of which has been either approved or is pending, covering some 180 miles. Last year approval was given to abandoning the line from Wolseley to Reston on which one of the grain companies had just the previous year completed a large terminal elevator. As to some of these lines with respect to which application has been made, the lines have been built within the last two years.
I think members are concerned about this matter, and they have a right to ask the government to give some heed to the recommendations of the MacPherson commission,

which said that if we are going to have a policy of abandonment it should be stated well in advance so that business people and the general public could lay their plans accordingly; that there should be a period of five years between the time the plan was issued and the time the abandonment took place; and that some policy of compensation ought to be worked out for those adversely affected.
What concerns the members from the prairies is the fact that the abandonments are proceeding. Applications are being made and in some cases are being granted. However, the over-all policy has not been announced and has not been implemented. The result is that when the policy is finally announced we may find that several of these lines have already been abandoned and the service discontinued.
I am not going to take the time of the committee to deal with this very time consuming problem. I know the Minister of Finance wants to get this resolution through, and I am prepared not to press it at this time. I simply raise it as an illustration of one of the kinds of problems that members must raise. If the government were prepared to send this kind of matter to a committee of the house, in this case the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, it would take much of the pressure off the house and would give members an opportunity to raise matters which are affecting their constituents without having to resort to lengthy question periods and to motions on going into supply or motions to adjourn the house to discuss matters of urgent public importance.
All I want to say is that we in this group are just as anxious as any other group in the house to press on with the business of the house, but I submit to the Prime Minister with great respect that the way to achieve that is not to suggest to the opposition that our best contribution is just to button our lips and let the government put through everything.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I am in agreement with the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet when he says he is very seldom in agreement with the things the Prime Minister proposes. I, too, find myself in that category. It may well be,

however, that his thoughts were translated incorrectly and if so, then I apologize.
In any event, I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and others who have dealt with this question of what parliament should be doing, how it should be approaching its business, reached the nub of the question when they made reference to the employment of our standing and special committees of the house. It is in this context that I should like to express a few thoughts about what parliament might do in the coming days to speed up or streamline consideration of some of the matters which will be before us.
I recall when the government was elected in 1958, with its massive 208 members, the Prime Minister made extensive reference to the necessity of putting the committees of parliament to work. We had, as members will recall who participated in them, committees meeting morning, noon and night. In some cases hon. members had to attend two or three committee meetings at the same time. There was a desire expressed by the Prime Minister four or five years ago to have the committees function to promote the conduct of parliamentary business in a proper manner. I feel those same views should hold true today, but we do not see that desire exemplified in processing matters through parliament and getting them to the particular committees.
I remember that when I was in the provincial legislature in British Columbia-and I believe the hon. member who is now here from Vancouver South was also in the legislature at that time and participated in some committees with me-one of the long standing practices there was to refer all municipal matters to a municipal affairs committee. All parties were represented on that committee, and the work of the legislative assembly in respect of municipal matters was done in the committee. When the committee reported to the house there was relatively little discussion, apart from general representations and comments by one member from each party. In this way the time the legislature spent in dealing with municipal legislation was relatively small, because the actual work had been done beforehand in the committee. I believe the same thing could very easily hold true here.
I should like to give one example of a subject matter that I think could be referred, and I hope will be referred, to a committee. I am pleased to note that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is here, because the subject deals with his department. In the last few years, particularly since the end of the war, we have seen a great increase in the movement of people in the world. We

have seen great advances in communications and in transportation to the point where our world, in one sense, is getting smaller and smaller. This greater movement of people in the world creates problems for different countries in so far as their immigration laws are concerned. Canada has not been exempted from problems in this particular field.
There is the whole question of the necessity to expand our industrial base in this country, and the consequent need to have a large enough population to enable industry to expand. This problem comes into conflict sometimes with the attitudes of governments in respect of immigration, the number of people who can come to Canada, the countries from which they can come and so on. We have the whole question of the relationship between immigration and employment possibilities which has been in a confused state for quite a long period of time, extending even beyond 1957. We have the question of the continual promises by this government concerning amendments to the Immigration Act, none of which have yet been implemented. However, these promises cause concern amongst the members here and cause questions to be asked in the house.
There is the whole question of the structure of our citizenship act; our attitude toward the number of people who have been deported and the number of these orders for deportation which have not been executed, about which I asked the other day. There is a sessional paper on this matter which indicates that almost 5,000 people have been ordered deported since 1957, but there are more than 1,500 of these orders which have not been executed. There is the question of the reasons given for the failure to execute these orders. This is something which it is highly desirable we should get into, become involved in and about which we should ask questions. In what better place could this happen than in a committee of this house which the departmental officials can attend?
There is the entire field of the investigation into the alleged illegal entry of Chinese people into this country, which investigation was abandoned just a few days ago. We have the whole question of the impact of that investigation upon the rights of citizens in Canada, and the question of the long delays which were experienced by people of Chinese origin applying for citizenship. Some of them had to wait two or three years before then-citizenship papers came through, even though they had passed the examination. There is the question of the two way approach to immigrants coming from Italy, which came to light a year or two ago. There is the question of refugees coming to this country

and the question of tubercular patients coming from other countries and being treated here.
Then there is the whole question of the department of Indian affairs and its attitudes, which was dealt with to some extent in the joint committee on Indian affairs which met for three years. The opportunity for this committee to go into departmental estimates and policy was not available, however, because the committee was concerned with briefs and presentations by groups of people from outside. Nevertheless the whole field of Indian affairs is another very important subject matter with which I think a committee should deal.
As a result of asking members who have been here for quite a number of years, I find that none of them can remember when the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration were referred to a committee for study. Perhaps that might have been the case 20 or 25 years ago, but so far as I am able to determine not since that time have these estimates been referred to a committee. I believe they should be, because it is in committee that we can inquire into the questions I have enumerated, and many more also. After all, we have a new minister, so let us have a new approach. Let us send this particular subject matter to a committee, and when that committee reports to parliament perhaps there will be relatively short discussion in the house, as has been the case when other departmental estimates were referred to committees.
One case which supports that contention is the estimates for the Department of Fisheries. For two successive years they were sent to a committee, and that happened since this government took office. We went into the estimates extensively in the committee and discussed all relevant matters with the officials. Then when the estimates came before the house, in committee of the whole, there were just very brief statements from members in each party and the estimates were passed without great delay.
I believe this should be done with the estimates for the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and that we should deal with such matters in the manner so ably outlined by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I hope his suggestions will be accepted by the government as a desirable course to follow rather than trying to legislate by exhaustion, as was outlined by the Prime Minister yesterday.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I might deal with that particular matter myself, as it covers two departments. However, before doing so I want to say to hon. gentlemen who participated in this discussion yesterday afternoon and today that all of them made an excellent contribution to a subject that is near and dear to hon. members in all parts of the house, namely the assurance that to the greatest extent possible parliament shall operate effectively and efficiently.
There was a suggestion made that if there were an extension of the hours that would be legislative consideration by exhaustion. I would simply point out the fact that in the United Kingdom parliament the sitting starts in the afternoon at either two o'clock or two thirty and runs through the period from six to eight o'clock, while we adjourn for dinner, and continues until adjournment, which is not automatic.
They have a much larger house, of course.

speechtext: I beg your pardon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister

That is true, but between six and eight o'clock there is a kind of unwritten law that hon. members have an opportunity of dealing with those things they desire to place before the house, and no votes are called at that time because the attendance is not such as would be conducive to a fair and proper declaration of the house's intention on any matter.
1 listened with interest to the suggestion that more should be done on the part of the government in placing these questions in the hands of committees. As one hon. gentleman pointed out, I had that view myself. I endeavoured to bring that about, and I was

criticized as strongly as it was possible for anyone to be criticized on a matter that should have been the least provocative of criticism. We found that the opposition members took a strong stand against committee work. At that time their objection was that they had insufficient members to man the various committees.
However, as one looks back over the matter I think one can agree with Mr. Mackenzie King who, on one occasion when approached by the opposition of which I was a member in the early days, in the 1940's, said that the committee system is not in keeping with the British tradition of government or the parliamentary system. I did not hold that view, and when I became Prime Minister I endeavoured to expand and extend the committee system; but on the basis of experience, and speaking as dispassionately as I can, I must say I am not at all as certain today as I was in 1958 that the committee system is the system to adopt under our parliamentary plan of government.
However, we have all shown a most desirable support of the objective of making parliament more effective and getting on with the business. It has always been the case since the forties, and I cannot go back beyond that, that for the first six, eight or nine weeks of a session it has been virtually impossible to secure the passage of very much legislation, and that trend has been intensified in consequence of the changes that were made. We endeavoured to improve the situation by holding meetings of the rules committee in successive years and, while there were a number of reforms brought in, I think in certain particulars it will be agreed that the result was to make the rules more inflexible and bring about the very antithesis of the objective that all hon. members had in mind.
I shall not go over again what I referred to yesterday in connection with the legislative program. Certainly one of the difficulties is to so organize-and that difficulty becomes intensified with the increased number of parties-the house that attention may be given to some of the problems that were referred to this afternoon in a very fair discussion of the subject by the leader of the New Democratic party.

I just could not understand the circumstances connected with the answer in question, and I had this matter looked into. I am going to place before the committee the record as it is. Yesterday the hon. member asked a question, which is to be found at page 1995 of Hansard, dealing with remissions of customs 27507-3-130

duties under the provisions of section 2 of the surcharge on imports order, P.C. 1962902. The answer was as follows:
The information requested is not available as detailed statistics are not maintained pertaining to the application of the surcharge on imports order. To present a complete answer would entail a careful examination of approximately 2,205,235 import entries passed at 276 ports of entry in Canada.
1 would point out that the applicable section of the Financial Administration Act, section 22(8), reads as follows:
A statement of each remission of one thousand dollars or more granted under this section shall be reported to the House of Commons in the public accounts.
That has been the course in the past. In order to ascertain what has constituted compliance with this requirement, the public accounts for the last 15 years have been carefully examined. Prior to the passing of the Financial Administration Act in 1951 it was the duty of the Auditor General, under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, to report remissions to parliament, but there were no upper or lower limitations based on the amounts of the remissions. As a matter of practice the Auditor General reported only those exceeding $1,000. In cases of a general remission applicable to classes of goods and not in terms of individual importers, he simply recorded a statement describing the nature of the remission and quoted the authority for it. The Financial Administration Act of 1951 incorporated the Auditor General's method of reporting and required the same kind of information he had been reporting to be henceforth included in the annual public accounts.
If hon. members will examine the public accounts they will find that this house has accepted the listing of remissions in excess of $1,000 which have been to the relief of individuals or corporations, but has made a distinction throughout the years between these and remissions of a general character extending to a broad sector of the community or to a particular commodity or class of commodities destined to a particular use in the public interest. In this latter case the house has accepted a statement-and I emphasize the word "statement"-as seems to be called for by the Financial Administration Act; that is, a statement giving the nature of the general remissions and the authority under which they were made effective. Obviously this statement is required because such broad remissions normally exceed $1,000. Besides the repeated acceptance by the house of this method of complying with the act, there has been equal acceptance by the committee on public accounts.

Interim Supply
Apart from the fact that the requirements of the statute can reasonably be interpreted and applied as they have been over the years, and that during this time the house has accepted the practice followed, there are eminently sound practical reasons for the practice adopted.
The present instance is one of a remission of a portion of import surcharges on broad classes of commodities. The Financial Administration Act, section 22(2), provides that a remission may be partial, conditional or unconditional and may be granted in any particular case or class of case and before the liability therefor arises. In practice this means that customs officers, where remission applies before the liability arises, do not make an assessment of the full levy that would have applied and then deduct the remission. They simply go straight ahead and take the net figure. To do otherwise would entail a tremendous amount of unnecessary work. Where, of course, the remission is an individual one and expressed in a sum certain, the calculation is made in detail, as it is in the case of a remission by way of a refund.
When I heard this matter raised yesterday I immediately went into this question, because there is one thing above everything else that must be upheld in the house; that is, the right of hon. members to information. That is something that, as the leader of this house, I will insist upon at all times. Because of that, when the hon. gentleman raised this matter I immediately secured the fullest information on the subject so as to ascertain the reason for this answer and to also ascertain whether or not it was of an unusual type. I recognized immediately that some would say there was an endeavour to conceal, and that the reason for that answer was that the government or the department had something to hide. However, I found- and I am glad to be able to report to the committee that I did-that in no case since 1951, when it became a matter of statutory enactment, and prior to that on the basis of the Auditor General's reports, had any other course been followed.
I am not hiding anything, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. gentleman or any other hon. member wishes to make a motion for information in this regard, we have nothing to conceal and the information will be furnished. But I want him, and everybody else who moves a motion, to recognize these facts: that to examine the records and list individual importations and individual importers will require over 125,000 man hours at a cost of $400,000 to $500,000. In addition to that, for the examination, segregation and listing of current entries, the cost would run at least from $80,000 to $85,000 a month. If the house wants

to do this and wishes to depart from what has been the practice in the past, then this government intends to accept its wishes, as it always should in the interests of sound parliamentary government. We have nothing to conceal. I will leave it to the house, and I will leave it to the hon. gentleman whether he feels that we should in this case, because of the circumstances under which this item in question came into existence in June last by order in council, under the authority of parliamentary practice, furnish this information. But I want him and anyone associated with him to recognize that it is a departure from the practice of the past, and what the cost will be to the treasury in consequence. In principle the present remission of surcharges is in the nature of a ceiling on import surcharges, applicable from the time of their imposition, on certain duties or classes of duties. The remission is of wide application and is not based on the relief of any particular organization, firm or individual.
Having placed that before the committee, if the hon. gentleman-he need not make a decision now-and those associated with him, and the house, wish the production of something that has not been asked in the past, then because of the particular circumstances under which this came into existence under the exchange order in council of June 24, 1962, the government will certainly comply. We do not want anyone to believe that there is anything being concealed; but I will point out that to follow that course is a tremendously costly procedure. As I have said, it will cost almost half a million dollars and will, in addition, cost $85,000 a month. I leave myself and the government entirely in the hands of the house, because we are not going to have it said that we concealed anything in connection with this matter.

I think a great deal of tune could have been saved if we had had discussions such as this, and more, much earlier in the session.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister indulges in something which I have seen happen in this house before. He suggests that a private member is asking information the obtaining of which is going to cost many thousands or many hundreds of thousands of dollars, and therefore the onus is put on that private member whether or not he wants to

have his question pursued. May I make it very clear that the cost of obtaining this information is not occasioned by the question I put on the order paper. My question has been answered; Mr. Speaker would so rule. The cost of obtaining this information is occasioned by section 22(8) of the Financial Administration Act, which in my view requires the government to obtain and to give the information in the public accounts. The only difference between my question and the law is that I asked for the information now for a three or four months period, whereas the law requires that this information be given at the end of the fiscal year in the public accounts.

I thank the Prime Minister for giving me the chance to draw attention to this. As I say, my point is that it is the law which requires this to be done, only the law requires it to be done after the end of the fiscal year instead of at this particular point in time. The Prime Minister said that in order to ascertain what the law means one must look to see what the practice has been-if I do him any injustice in putting it that way, he can correct me. He said that the records have been checked since 1951. I have not checked every year, but I have checked a good many of them. The Prime Minister said that on checking the records he found only in certain kinds of instances are the individual items given. What I have before me are the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1961, and in them are a long list of items over $1,000 remitted under the provisions of section 22 of the Financial Administration Act with respect to the Department of National Revenue. It is also true, as the Prime Minister has said, that there are a number of instances, a dozen or so, on pages 37-5 and 37-6 of this volume where there is merely a recital of an order in council that authorized remissions in certain particular classes or cases. For example, P.C. 1959-15/1504, November 11, 1959, authorized the remission of excise duty sales and excise taxes on cigarettes purchased by the province of Ontario for distribution as Christmas gifts to members of the armed services of all countries stationed in the province. Another example is P.C. 1960-31/440, April 7, 1960, which authorized the remission of taxes on various items of equipment imported from the United States for use in the study of geophysical phenomena during the 27507-3-130i
Interim Supply
international geophysical year January 1 to December 31, 1959. And there are others of that kind.
The point I am making is that using the line of argument which the Prime Minister used, namely that one has to look at the records to see what had been done previously in order to determine what ought to be done now, I do not find any case where there is a record of an order in council for remissions which were given at the same time and in the same order in council which imposed the tax. That is what we have in this surcharge on imports order. We have one order which, under the provisions of one statute, raises the duties and then at the same time, under the provisions of another statute, purports to lower those duties. I think the Prime Minister let the cat out of the bag with the language which he used a moment ago, when he said -he will correct me if I do not use his language correctly-that this remission is, in effect, a ceiling or a limit on the amount by which the customs duties have been raised. When I say that that is letting the cat out of the bag, what I mean is that the Prime Minister is admitting that this order is a case of doing indirectly what the government did not have the power to do directly.
This whole situation that the government is in-the difficulty it faces, the fact that it will cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to keep the law under section 22(8) of the Financial Administration Act

arises from the fact that it operated on the basis of an order in council of doubtful validity and that it failed to bring the matter before parliament. If the Prime Minister had done what I understood him to mean he would do when he spoke on television on June 24, and had brought this matter before parliament for validation or confirmation by legislation, we would not be in this position at all. But the government has operated on the basis of an order in council, a hodgepodge of a thing based on two statutes, a procedure which has put the government in an impossible situation. I am not surprised to learn that it would cost these tremendous sums of money to get this information. In fact, I think it is just about impossible to get the kind of information for which I asked in my question the other day. I expected that at some point the answer would be that this kind of information could not be obtained. What this points up is, as I say, the fact that the government has operated on a basis on which it had no right to operate.
If I may go back to this point again, may I say this. The Prime Minister recites the law. He reads section 22, subsection 8. He admits it is the law and he admits that it

Interim Supply
should be kept. Then he says, "How has it been kept since 1951?" It has been kept by having in some cases individual items, but in other cases just a recital that an order in council granted a remission in certain particular cases. However, those remissions were all the repayment of taxes that were otherwise statutory or that were otherwise legal. What we have here, however, is a case of giving with one hand and taking with the other. Unless there is some one that I have not found in the public accounts since 1951, I will say that there is not a precedent for this kind of double barrelled order in council.
It is that kind of difficulty which the government has got itself into. It could still get out of it by bringing the matter before parliament in the form of proper legislation. If it is not prepared to do that, at least there is one other thing it could do; and I would hope that the Prime Minister, having regard to the conciliatory manner in which he has spoken today, will give consideration to the terms of the amendment to the third reading of another bill that is before the house. I think if that amendment could be accepted by the government and accepted by the house and if that bill could go to the committee on banking and commerce, then the whole thing could be discussed, people could be called, and we could get this thing sorted out.
I say again that I am not embarrassed by the Prime Minister's suggestion that I must make the decision whether I ask that half a million dollars be spent on getting information that would more fully answer the question I asked the other day. I give the answer right now. I have no intention of asking that that be done. However, I say this to the government. The fact that I have no intention of asking that it should be done does not relieve the government from facing up, on its own, to the question of what the law demands of it, and facing up to the question of what the Auditor General will say a year or so from now when he discovers that section 22, subsection 8, has not been complied with in respect of an operation for which there is no precedent.
It is still my view that the whole question of the surcharges should be brought before parliament for validation or whatever parliament chooses to do with them. Failing that I appeal to the government. I realize, Mr. Chairman, that I am a wee bit out of order so I will say it quickly and sit down because this is the subject of another debate. When we get to the third reading of the bill amending the Customs Tariff I hope the Prime Minister will suggest that the house accept the amendment moved by my leader and allow

this matter to be referred to the committee on banking and commerce so that it can be sorted out there.

Mr. Chairman, there is an item here asking for two twelfths of vote 213a for the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. I wish to raise a problem to which I should like some consideration given. It has to do with the changing of schedules by Canadian National Railways. For some period of time there has been a great deal of comment about Canadian National's trains Nos. 3 and 4 known as the Continental, which run from Montreal to Vancouver. Service on parts of this run is now being discontinued, and I am particularly interested in the section between Capreol and Montreal.

What is being done in this case is very interesting because the act is very definite that when one line crosses another line there should be reasonable meets between trains and reasonable facilities for passengers using these lines. In this particular case the Canadian National Railways have bastardized the time schedule to such an extent there will not be any passengers left on that line. Then, Canadian National will be able to go to the board of transport commissioners and say, we have no passengers so this line should be discontinued.
My feeling, Mr. Chairman, is that we should not allow them to do this. This train made a 15-minute meet with the Ontario Northland Railway which enabled travellers from northern Ontario and northern Quebec to go to Ottawa and Montreal. By changing the time of this train, the railway will ultimately eliminate this passenger service entirely. The only passengers using this service in the last few weeks have been a few people going to stations close to North Bay. This train now leaves at the unreasonable hour of 4.50 in the morning.
This problem was raised in the committee, and I am not in agreement with the argument made at that time by the president of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Gordon. I think he should go back to banking and quit trying to run a railroad. The people in my area are very perturbed and feel they are not going to have any jobs about a year from now. There is no question in my mind but that the railway is going to be able to go to the board of transport commissioners and say, we want to discontinue trains Nos. 3 and 4 because these trains serve no purpose whatever. The railway will be able to prove these trains are not carrying any passengers.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, this parliament has a responsibility to the workers on the railway and to the people of this country to supply a passenger service. There is no question in my mind but that passenger service is of no value to the railway, and it costs the railway money to operate this service. However, we are asked to give assistance to the railways in the form of freight subsidies. In fact, we are asked to give all types of assistance to the railways so that they will be able to operate. I suggest to the management of Canadian National Railways that I, personally, am going to make it my business to hold up their estimates or any other grants from this parliament until they decide they are going to give some kind of service to the people of this

country. I used this service as an example because it is the one about which I am aware.
When Canadian National Railways come before parliament and ask to carry mail, then I am going to look at that request in the light of the needs of my constituents in northern Ontario. If the railway is not serving these people in northern Ontario, then be damned as far as I am concerned with their request to carry mail or anything else that is going to make them money. I think it is about time we took a look at this situation. Every time the railway comes here asking for a new line, then I am going to look at this request. Unless they are going to give some consideration to the needs of the people for transportation, then let us get rid of the railway and substitute for that some other form of service so that the people in the transportation industry will have jobs and the people in the country will be given the service they are not now getting.
We know, Mr. Chairman, that the railway will go to the board of transport commissioners and say, this is the condition in which we find ourselves now. I am satisfied that less than a month ago the railway decided that it was going to create conditions that would allow it to go to the board of transport commissioners in a few months and say the situation had reached a stage where the railway must drop that line. Anyone in Canada who has watched the machinations of the railway over the past year in connection with these trains Nos. 3 and 4, and the conniving that has been done with the Canadian Pacific with relation to these particular trains, will know that the ultimate goal is the discontinuation of these passenger trains.
I believe that now is the time for us to take a look at this problem. I will be quite prepared, Mr. Chairman, when their estimates come before us again or when they ask for more assistance, to ask a number of members who are interested in the over-all transportation policy of this country, to hold up the passage of those estimates until such time as we get a much clearer picture of the transportation possibilities in the future. I believe that we give the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways enough consideration that they should give the people of this country some consideration.
I talked to a railway superintendent the other day who was telling me about all the consideration the railway was giving to shippers in respect of new cars that were going to be put in service for a new ore operation. However, he could not give me any encouragement when I asked him about the installation of air conditioning in a restaurant car on this particular railway because he said
Ways and Means
it was going to cost money and the railway was now losing money on this operation. If the railways concerned are not going to try to co-operate to serve the needs of the travelling public in this country, then why should we help them in some other area which might make them some money? If the railways are not going to help the passengers, to whom they should be giving some consideration, then I do not believe we should give them any consideration.
Let us take a look at the operations of trains Nos. 3 and 4. The train used to leave Ottawa in the late evening and arrive in North Bay at three o'clock in the morning. The passengers did not have to get off the train because their sleeper was picked up and they went on their way to Timmins, Noranda or other points in northern Ontario or northern Quebec. The car was attached to an Ontario Northland Railway train and the people could sleep until nine o'clock. Then, what happened? The first move was to cut off that sleeper, but they left one car that went from North Bay up on the Ontario Northland Railway. Then, they decided they would cut off that North Bay car and it would no longer go on the Ontario Northland Railway. The railway gave us some cock and bull story about how much it costs to drag that particular car behind the train. However, it did not cost any more for the porter, and it did not make them any more money because the Ontario Northland Railway did not get any money out of it. The passengers who had to be wakened at North Bay and sent into the coach said, to heck with it, we will use some other method of transportation. Then, the railway parks this car at North Bay and when the train comes back it picks the car up and takes it to Montreal. This arrangement worked fairly well for the people who lived in North Bay or who wanted to do business in North Bay. They could do business in North Bay during the day, go to the sleeping car and by the time it was picked up by the train they already had a few hours sleep. Then, this car was no longer available, either. Now, there is a further move and the time of departure of this train is changed to ten minutes to five in the morning. It arrives in Montreal at three o'clock in the afternoon and in Ottawa at 11.30 in the morning.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, who is going to ride on this train? Perhaps an Indian who has been out on a drunk all night and wants to go to Algonquin park to sober up, might ride it. I talked to some people around the station at North Bay and they said they presumed that this was the only type of person who was going to catch that train.

This couple were married in Austria on May 21, 1955. While I have not had the opportunity of looking at the evidence in this particular case, I presume that the other place was given a copy of the marriage certificate from that country and that it ascertained that it had been in good order and that a marriage, in fact, had taken place. We are concerned with this matter, Mr. Speaker, for this reason. One of these days somebody is going to come to parliament and get a divorce when in fact he was never married in the first place. This is something that could easily arise. You may wonder why we refer to this matter, Mr. Speaker. May I say that it is quite possible for a person using a marriage certificate from another country to come before parliament, use another person who was not his wife, and be divorced from the second person where the wife in the particular case was not the person named in the marriage certificate. This would be much easier, I would think, if the marriage had taken place outside the country. This would result in the acceptance of a petition and the disallowance of a marriage which possibly never existed at all between the parties asking for the divorce.
While it is true that the marriage took place in 1955, may I say that in my part of the country there are many people living who are married and who came to this country in about the year 1928, where there is no possibility of their getting a divorce. I can foresee the arrangement that could be made if we were not particularly careful about proving that the people obtaining the divorce were the same people who originally married. I would suggest that this may not be true in this case because of the date, namely 1955. However, by way of an example, let us consider a marriage certificate which was obtained in a divorce action and which was dated somewhere prior to 1928, particularly if only one of the parties to that marriage had come to this country. The necessity of making an arrangement here would probably be indicated to anyone, considering the fact that our arrangements with these countries, particularly those behind the iron curtain, would not allow us to get the information we would otherwise have. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to have the opportunity of moving this resolution tonight. I should like at the outset to give the reasons why the government has decided to ask parliament for authority to establish a national economic development board. The government is determined that this country will continue to prosper and to grow. It is determined to stimulate the further expansion of our existing industries and to encourage even further the development in Canada of new and efficient industries. In this way we will provide new and increasing opportunities for Canadians in all walks of life for rewarding employment and ever-improving standards of living.
nology we chose in defining this board. It will be national because it will be concerned with all parts of Canada, as well, of course, as with Canada as a whole. Its scope will be the 3 million square miles of this nation and the geographical regions and economic sectors which comprise it. Its scope will be economic because its concern will be with the soundest, most productive and most prosperous use of Canadian economic resources. On the human side it will contribute to the aim of a good life in Canada, to the provision of economic opportunities for every Canadian. This board will also be in harmony with the aims and programs of this government, which I think it is fair to say are a part of the great movement in Canada toward national unity and development. There is nothing particularly new, Mr. Chairman, in looking forward to these goals because this government in the past five years has brought forward a broad and workable program of economic measures: in the field of trade, a major program of export promotion and financing; in the resource fields, new policies for expansion in oil and gas, energy, forestry and fisheries development; in the competitive health of the economy, policies ranging from fixing at the proper rate the external value of the Canadian dollar to stimulating an awareness for the need of productivity gain in Canadian industry; in agriculture, remarkable strides in farm improvements, marketing and finance; in the public sector, a whole new program of co-operation with provincial and municipal governments to build up the basic social capital of this nation; and, in our most important resource, a determined effort to provide employment opportunities and high standards of living by new break-throughs, such as the technical training program, and by far sighted measures such as the one introduced last week by my colleague the Minister of Labour in undertaking research into the impact of automation and technological change on jobs and employment.
These policies, and the advances that have followed from their implementation, have been directed largely to specific areas of the economy and to meet specific needs very often too long ignored. Today we are broadening our canvas. We are looking at Canada as a whole-at what its economy is now; what it is likely to be; where the opportunities for growth seem greatest; where the deep-rooted problems that must be solved are located, and how they can be solved. I am opening up this discussion in these terms, Mr. Chairman, because I think that in this country, and especially in this house with its present composition, we need a new national
2074	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board awareness, a new national interest on forward, constructive terms. It is within this context that I shall be discussing this new, and to some extent almost revolutionary, proposal for the establishment of a national economic development board.
Above all, the government is determined that this country will continue to prosper and grow. We have two clear objectives in mind: to stimulate the further expansion of our industries, and to encourage even further the development in Canada of new and efficient industries. We are by no means dissatisfied with the progress we are making in these important fields. By comparison with other countries we Canadians have good reason to be proud of our record of economic growth and achievement. This record does not mean that we should not strive for an even better performance. We will face major changes in the world economy in the years ahead which will affect production and employment in this country. We are still in the process of extending our frontiers, developing our resources, and consolidating the gains we have made in the past. We must be prepared for more changes and developments in the immediate future and, I might say, Mr. Chairman, in the far reaching future.
This new board will help us to meet these developments and guide us to our opportunities. Its role will be advisory, and I say that emphatically; but its advice will have a great influence not only on government economic policy but on economic thinking in the nation. This board will help us to draw on the best ideas and the most up to date information to help the government achieve an ever-widening and prosperous economy in all parts of the country.
This advice will come forward to the government, Mr. Chairman, I would think, under three main headings. First the board will investigate, analyse and report on the medium and longer term prospects and possibilities of the Canadian economy as a whole, and of particular industries and areas. In this sense, its findings will be like sign posts or guide lines for progress and expansion. Second, the board will study and report on the methods and measures which will stimulate the development in Canada of new and efficient industries to help Canada grow. Its recommendations will cut across the whole range of government fiscal, monetary, commercial and economic policy, and give the government the opportunity to look at the future effects of these policies on our economy. Third, the board will look into new projects and measures whether in the public or in the private sector of the economy, and make recommendations to the government
[Mr. Nowlan.l

about those which are likely to make an important contribution to the growth and development of the national economy.
In addition to seeking, analysing and recommending ways and means for development in the domestic economy, the board should be able to bring forward useful proposals and worth-while advice on such major problems in the economy as our balance of payments position. I have stressed these problems in the house before during this session, and I suspect, Mr. Chairman, that I will be doing so again from time to time. We must increase our trade surplus and reduce our dependence on foreign capital, no matter how welcome this investment may be. There are no easy solutions and there are no quick solutions; but if we are to correct the problems of the last decade and a half, we must begin now to solve these problems and at least attempt to work out solutions.
As a result, there is now in Canada a widespread view, and one that this government shares, that there is a need for a new instrument to bring together leaders in management, labour, finance, industry and agriculture as well as spokesmen for the public interest generally, so that their collective advice, based on the most complete and up to date information available, and stemming from a common cause, can be made available to the government in the carrying out of its responsibilities to help Canada fulfil its economic potential in the future. This new instrument to which I am referring tonight, of which this resolution is the forerunner, will ensure a flow of ideas and proposals in both directions. This is especially important at a time when the world economy is undergoing great and rapid changes. There are dramatic changes in technology which in turn dictate new changes in business organization.
There are important new developments, too, in commercial policy and in international trading arrangements. Canada will have to find ways of adapting itself to the new trading world which is emerging. I simply suggest there that one of the noteworthy achievements of the last few months is the success of the President of the United States in having had the congress of that country adopt a tariff policy which should result in lower tariffs in the United States and a wider trading area, and also the imagination of our own Prime Minister in bringing before the conference in London the suggestion of a wider trading area and now the welcome of that suggestion by the President of the United States. There is the danger being excluded from markets which heretofore have been ours,

National Economic Development Board
and the necessity of developing a world wide, or at least a world trading area. This is one of the necessities with which this country is confronted, and is one of the problems requiring advice and guidance in the years ahead. It is one of the problems on which I think this council or this board may give us great assistance.
Of course it is obvious that the success of the board will depend largely on the quality and type of persons who are selected to guide its work. The chairman will be definitely a very key figure. It is the intention that this person shall devote all of his time or give all of his time to the work of the board. He will also be the chief executive officer and guide the work of the expert, well qualified, well remunerated staff. He must be a person of recognized national standing, of mature judgment, with close and continuing contacts throughout the broad range of the Canadian community. He will necessarily, of course, lean heavily on the knowledge and experience of the board. These members will be appointed from among the recognized leaders in the many and varied fields of Canadian economic life.
At a later stage when the house will be examining the legislation in detail, it will be more appropriate to speak of the arrangements for the staff which will be required for the efficient conduct of the board's work. I would make only one comment now. As well as having a permanent staff, the board should be able to hire personnel with special qualifications on a temporary basis, so that highly skilled persons from universities, from industry and from other private organizations should be able to make their services available to the board at the staff level as well as at the board level.
Let me develop for a moment what I consider to be the heart of the board's work. It is really quite simple to state: advice to government-and again I stress the fact-on ways in which to achieve the highest possible levels of growth and development. This new government body will be able to look a little further ahead and to study and advise on economic trends and on the likely shape of the economy over a period of, say, three, five or ten years.
As members of the house are well aware, in the day to day work of government-and I am sure my hon. friends opposite who have had experience in government recognize this fact-ministers and their advisers within the government service are very often not able to find the time in which to take an over-all look at our economic prospects and possibilities. They are responsible for departmental administration and for the problems of their
departments. Fortunately we have many well qualified and expert economic advisers, economists and civil servants generally in the government employ. I know of no country which is more fortunately blessed than we are in that connection. But in almost every case these people, these men, these women, are responsible for administrative problems, for day to day decisions within their own departments; and looking after those matters, and looking after them adequately and as well as they do, they have not the time in which to look over the whole broad horizon of the national problems even of today, let alone those which might arise tomorrow or five years or ten years from now.
So what we need at the moment and what this board presages and assumes is that we will be able to set up a board not restricted to departmental details, not restricted to dealing with the problems of the moment-because those will be dealt with by the civil servants in the various departments-but applying the highest levels of professional skills which can be obtained to advise the government on the sort of problems we are likely to face in the future, and how in their opinion we can best be prepared to deal with them.
The government is determined to play its full part in developing and encouraging a high level of economic growth in Canada. It can only do this if it has available to it information and advice on which right policies and actions must be based. It is a key function of this board to formulate advice to government on which policies for growth and development can be based.
We believe that what is now needed is a more systematic and comprehensive apparatus for examining proposals for such projects. In the past many proposals-as hon. gentlemen who have had experience of government well know-come before them on an ad hoc basis. They are recommended by responsible parties. They obviously have merit apparently at the moment, and one is apt to deal with them on a specialized or ad hoc basis rather than in connection with the whole economy of the country.

I accept my hon. friend's statement on that matter, he having had much experience on this matter in years gone by. Some were examined within the existing organization of government and some occasionally had been examined by royal commissions especially constituted for the purpose of making a report on specific problems. It is our view that the national economic development board can make an important
2076	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board contribution by examining proposals for national economic development projects on a continuing basis, to help establish priorities and to advise on how particular projects fit into our over-all economic needs.
The government will wish on occasion to refer particular proposals to the national economic development board for examination and report. In its examination and report the board will be expected to look into the economic and financial feasibility of such projects, into the cost of such projects and to compare these costs with the national benefits which will accrue, and to develop recommendations accordingly. But it is important also that the board have the authority to take initiatives in this field; to examine any projects or proposals which come to its attention from sources outside the government. The broad representative character of the board will enable it to be particularly effective in this field.
I should like to conclude my statement by emphasizing that the task of the board must be defined and its work related to the Canadian economy and to the Canadian situation. There is much talk about the success in other countries of economic development bodies which might too easily be assumed to be the same as the proposed economic development board which we are suggesting should be adopted by this house.
In considering this matter we have had very much in mind that the United Kingdom and other countries in western Europe have had experience in this field and we have taken considerable pains to draw on their experience. Members of the house will recall that the chairman of the national productivity council organized a special mission to Europe for the purpose of studying and evaluating the work of such bodies in a number of western European countries. We have had the benefit of their detailed report. We welcomed it and we have made a very careful study of it and have made use of it in drafting the legislation which will be submitted to the house, should the committee decide to adopt the resolution which I have presented.
Let me add immediately, Mr. Chairman, and let me emphasize this, that while we were able to draw from the British experience, the French experience and the experience of other European countries much that was good and much that was relevant, we also discovered that in many important respects the Canadian situation is unique and requires solutions and treatment which are definitely Canadian.
One very obvious thing, of course, in the light of our constitutional background, is that Canada is a federal state and a Canadian


development board must take this into consideration. That in itself makes the situation much different from boards which may be and have been set up in unitary states in various parts of western Europe. Again, in this country we have developed largely on a private enterprise basis. We have less government owned enterprise and much more private enterprise than is the case in many European countries today. Generally speaking, there is a good deal more direct government intervention and government participation in the economic and financial markets in those countries than there is in Canada, more, I suspect, than Canadians would want to have prevalent at this time and, I would hope, in the future.
But what all this comes to is that while we can learn from others we must develop our own methods and institutions designed to meet our own problems and needs. The national economic development board must be a uniquely Canadian organization. If not, it will not serve the purposes of Canada as we hope and expect it will.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that while some members of the house may not entirely agree with our idea of the role that government can best play in our economy, all members of the house would like to see Canada achieve the highest possible rate of growth and the highest possible levels of production and employment. In terms of these vital objectives I am sure we are all united and so, Mr. Chairman, I commend to this committee and to the house the proposal for a national economic development board. If the board succeeds in achieving the purposes which those of us who have thought of this and who have developed it have in mind, then I think that the introduction of this measure in the house tonight may be looked upon many years in the future as one of the occasions when the parliament of Canada contributed substantially, and much, to the development of the Canadian economy and the Canadian nation.
